claim: Biological membranes are usually formed by lipid bilayers.
source: Biological membranes create compartments, and are usually formed by lipid bilayers.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the abstract.

claim: In hyperthermophilic archaea that live optimally at temperatures above 80°C, membranes are monolayers which resemble fused bilayers.
source: However, in hyperthermophilic archaea that live optimally at temperatures above 80°C the membranes are monolayers which resemble fused bilayers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about archaeal membranes.

claim: AFV1 is a filamentous virus of Acidianus hospitalis that is enveloped with a lipid-containing membrane.
source: Many double-stranded DNA viruses which parasitize such hosts, including the filamentous virus AFV1 of Acidianus hospitalis, are enveloped with a lipid-containing membrane.
evidence: This is stated as background information about AFV1.

claim: The membrane in AFV1 is a ~2 nm-thick monolayer.
source: Using cryo-EM, we show that the membrane in AFV1 is a ~2 nm-thick monolayer, approximately half the expected membrane thickness, formed by host membrane-derived lipids which adopt a U-shaped 'horseshoe' conformation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The AFV1 membrane is approximately half the expected membrane thickness.
source: Using cryo-EM, we show that the membrane in AFV1 is a ~2 nm-thick monolayer, approximately half the expected membrane thickness, formed by host membrane-derived lipids which adopt a U-shaped 'horseshoe' conformation.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the measured thickness from cryo-EM data.

claim: The AFV1 membrane is formed by host membrane-derived lipids which adopt a U-shaped 'horseshoe' conformation.
source: Using cryo-EM, we show that the membrane in AFV1 is a ~2 nm-thick monolayer, approximately half the expected membrane thickness, formed by host membrane-derived lipids which adopt a U-shaped 'horseshoe' conformation.
evidence: This is a primary finding combining cryo-EM data with molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The unusual viral envelope structure results from the extreme curvature of the viral capsid.
source: We hypothesize that this unusual viral envelope structure results from the extreme curvature of the viral capsid, as 'horseshoe' lipid conformations favor such curvature and host membrane lipids that permit horseshoe conformations are selectively recruited into the viral envelope.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis based on the structural findings.

claim: 'Horseshoe' lipid conformations favor extreme curvature.
source: We hypothesize that this unusual viral envelope structure results from the extreme curvature of the viral capsid, as 'horseshoe' lipid conformations favor such curvature and host membrane lipids that permit horseshoe conformations are selectively recruited into the viral envelope.
evidence: This is stated as part of the hypothesis and supported by theoretical considerations.

claim: Host membrane lipids that permit horseshoe conformations are selectively recruited into the viral envelope.
source: We hypothesize that this unusual viral envelope structure results from the extreme curvature of the viral capsid, as 'horseshoe' lipid conformations favor such curvature and host membrane lipids that permit horseshoe conformations are selectively recruited into the viral envelope.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by lipid composition analysis.

claim: The AFV1 membrane can survive the most aggressive conditions involving extremes of temperature and pH.
source: The unusual envelope found in AFV1 also has many implications for biotechnology, since this membrane can survive the most aggressive conditions involving extremes of temperature and pH.
evidence: This is inferred from the natural habitat of the virus and known properties of archaeal lipids.

claim: The membrane is considered to be an adaptation to the host that has been convergently acquired in different virus orders.
source: The membrane is considered to be an adaptation to the host that has been convergently acquired in different virus orders (Buchmann and Holmes, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Hyperthermophilic archaeal viruses of the order Ligamenvirales contain non-enveloped, rigid rod-shaped viruses of the family Rudiviridae and enveloped, flexible filamentous viruses of the family Lipothrixviridae.
source: One example is provided by hyperthermophilic archaeal viruses of the order Ligamenvirales (Prangishvili and Krupovic, 2012) which contain non-enveloped, rigid rod-shaped viruses of the family Rudiviridae and enveloped, flexible filamentous viruses of the family Lipothrixviridae.
evidence: This is stated as established taxonomic knowledge with citation.

claim: Viruses from Rudiviridae and Lipothrixviridae families have many homologous genes and build their virions using structurally similar major capsid proteins.
source: Viruses from these two families have many homologous genes and build their virions using structurally similar major capsid proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these viral families.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of SIRV2 has been determined at ~4 Å resolution.
source: The ~4 Å-resolution cryo-EM structure (DiMaio et al., 2015) of a less-complex rudivirus, the Sulfolobus islandicus rod-shaped virus 2 (SIRV2) (Prangishvili et al., 1999), has shown that the viral double-stranded (ds) DNA is completely insulated from the external medium by the single capsid protein which transforms the viral DNA into A-form, explaining the stability of rudiviruses in extremely aggressive (80°C, pH 3) natural habitats.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: In SIRV2, the viral double-stranded DNA is completely insulated from the external medium by the single capsid protein which transforms the viral DNA into A-form.
source: The ~4 Å-resolution cryo-EM structure (DiMaio et al., 2015) of a less-complex rudivirus, the Sulfolobus islandicus rod-shaped virus 2 (SIRV2) (Prangishvili et al., 1999), has shown that the viral double-stranded (ds) DNA is completely insulated from the external medium by the single capsid protein which transforms the viral DNA into A-form, explaining the stability of rudiviruses in extremely aggressive (80°C, pH 3) natural habitats.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous structural work.

claim: The DNA insulation by capsid protein explains the stability of rudiviruses in extremely aggressive (80°C, pH 3) natural habitats.
source: The ~4 Å-resolution cryo-EM structure (DiMaio et al., 2015) of a less-complex rudivirus, the Sulfolobus islandicus rod-shaped virus 2 (SIRV2) (Prangishvili et al., 1999), has shown that the viral double-stranded (ds) DNA is completely insulated from the external medium by the single capsid protein which transforms the viral DNA into A-form, explaining the stability of rudiviruses in extremely aggressive (80°C, pH 3) natural habitats.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural data cited.

claim: Virions of lipothrixviruses are built from two paralogous major capsid proteins (MCP1 and MCP2) which bind dsDNA to form the nucleocapsid.
source: Virions of lipothrixviruses are more complex and are built from two paralogous major capsid proteins (MCP1 and MCP2) which bind dsDNA to form the nucleocapsid (Goulet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: The nucleocapsid of lipothrixviruses is enveloped by a lipid membrane.
source: The nucleocapsid is enveloped by a lipid membrane and the termini of the virion are decorated with specialized structures involved in host recognition (Bettstetter et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: The termini of lipothrixvirus virions are decorated with specialized structures involved in host recognition.
source: The nucleocapsid is enveloped by a lipid membrane and the termini of the virion are decorated with specialized structures involved in host recognition (Bettstetter et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Membranes of hyperthermophilic archaea often consist of unusual tetraether lipids, which form monolayers rather than bilayers typical of bacterial and eukaryotic membranes.
source: Membranes of hyperthermophilic archaea often consist of unusual tetraether lipids, which form monolayers rather than bilayers typical of bacterial and eukaryotic membranes (De Rosa and Gambacorta, 1988; Valentine, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Archaeal tetraether membranes are more rigid and stable than typical bilayers.
source: It has been demonstrated that such membranes are more rigid and stable than typical bilayers, a property with considerable biotechnological appeal.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Molecular details of membrane remodeling in archaea remain grossly understudied.
source: However, molecular details of membrane remodeling in archaea remain grossly understudied, and how a virus captures a non-bilayer membrane from its host is virtually unknown and is conceptually difficult to reconcile with our current understanding of membrane remodeling by viruses infecting eukaryotes (Harrison, 2008, 2015; Hurley and Hanson, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: How a virus captures a non-bilayer membrane from its host is virtually unknown.
source: However, molecular details of membrane remodeling in archaea remain grossly understudied, and how a virus captures a non-bilayer membrane from its host is virtually unknown and is conceptually difficult to reconcile with our current understanding of membrane remodeling by viruses infecting eukaryotes (Harrison, 2008, 2015; Hurley and Hanson, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: AFV1 virions are significantly more flexible than those of SIRV2, both with respect to bending as well as extension and compression.
source: Determining the structure of AFV1 was complicated by the fact that the virions are significantly more flexible, both with respect to bending as well as extension and compression, than those of SIRV2.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: AFV1 segments could be classified by the pitch of the prominent helix which ranged from 39 to 47 Å.
source: Segments could be classified by the pitch of the prominent helix which ranged from 39 to 47 Å (Figure 2), in contrast to the rather fixed pitch of 42 Å in SIRV2 (DiMaio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM data and shown in Figure 2.

claim: SIRV2 has a rather fixed pitch of 42 Å.
source: Segments could be classified by the pitch of the prominent helix which ranged from 39 to 47 Å (Figure 2), in contrast to the rather fixed pitch of 42 Å in SIRV2 (DiMaio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work on SIRV2.

claim: The 'gold standard' FSC yields an overall resolution of 4.1 Å for the AFV1 reconstruction.
source: Nevertheless, the 'gold standard' FSC (Figure 4) yields an overall resolution of 4.1 Å.
evidence: This is calculated from the FSC curve shown in Figure 4.

claim: The actual resolution of the AFV1 reconstruction is estimated to be ~4.5 Å.
source: We think that this is overly optimistic, and may arise from strong features in the DNA (Figure 5) (given the higher MW of the phosphates, the contrast is greater than for protein). A reasonable estimate (based upon comparison with the atomic model) is ~4.5 Å, but it is clear that parts of the complex (such as the outer helices facing the membrane, Figure 3b) are at a worse resolution, while other parts (such as the helix-turn-helix motifs on the very inside, Figure 3c) are at a better resolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with the atomic model.

claim: The outer diameter of the AFV1 virion is ~185 Å.
source: The outer diameter of the virion is ~185 Å, while the diameter of the nucleoprotein core alone (excluding the membrane) is ~135 Å.
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The diameter of the AFV1 nucleoprotein core alone (excluding the membrane) is ~135 Å.
source: The outer diameter of the virion is ~185 Å, while the diameter of the nucleoprotein core alone (excluding the membrane) is ~135 Å.
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The AFV1 membrane is only ~20–25 Å thick.
source: Surprisingly, the membrane is only ~20–25 Å thick, compared to ~40 Å found for archaeal tetraether monolayer (Valentine, 2007) membranes (Chong et al., 2003; Chugunov et al., 2014) and the 40–60 Å found for other cellular membranes and the viral envelopes derived from them (Hollinshead et al., 1999), but a crude calculation done by integrating the cryo-EM density (which corresponds to the Coulombic potential but will be roughly proportional to mass) suggests that ~40% of the total mass of the virion is due to the membrane.
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: Archaeal tetraether monolayer membranes are ~40 Å thick.
source: Surprisingly, the membrane is only ~20–25 Å thick, compared to ~40 Å found for archaeal tetraether monolayer (Valentine, 2007) membranes (Chong et al., 2003; Chugunov et al., 2014) and the 40–60 Å found for other cellular membranes and the viral envelopes derived from them (Hollinshead et al., 1999), but a crude calculation done by integrating the cryo-EM density (which corresponds to the Coulombic potential but will be roughly proportional to mass) suggests that ~40% of the total mass of the virion is due to the membrane.
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Other cellular membranes and viral envelopes derived from them are 40–60 Å thick.
source: Surprisingly, the membrane is only ~20–25 Å thick, compared to ~40 Å found for archaeal tetraether monolayer (Valentine, 2007) membranes (Chong et al., 2003; Chugunov et al., 2014) and the 40–60 Å found for other cellular membranes and the viral envelopes derived from them (Hollinshead et al., 1999), but a crude calculation done by integrating the cryo-EM density (which corresponds to the Coulombic potential but will be roughly proportional to mass) suggests that ~40% of the total mass of the virion is due to the membrane.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Approximately 40% of the total mass of the AFV1 virion is due to the membrane.
source: Surprisingly, the membrane is only ~20–25 Å thick, compared to ~40 Å found for archaeal tetraether monolayer (Valentine, 2007) membranes (Chong et al., 2003; Chugunov et al., 2014) and the 40–60 Å found for other cellular membranes and the viral envelopes derived from them (Hollinshead et al., 1999), but a crude calculation done by integrating the cryo-EM density (which corresponds to the Coulombic potential but will be roughly proportional to mass) suggests that ~40% of the total mass of the virion is due to the membrane.
evidence: This is calculated by integrating the cryo-EM density.

claim: The buoyant density for AFV1 virions was previously determined using a CsCl gradient and was consistent with other membrane-enveloped dsDNA viruses.
source: The buoyant density for the AFV1 virions was previously determined using a CsCl gradient (Bettstetter et al., 2003), and it was consistent with other membrane-enveloped dsDNA viruses (King et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The helically-averaged AFV1 membrane shows two clear density peaks, with the highest one on the outside and a lower one at inner radius.
source: The helically-averaged membrane shows two clear density peaks, with the highest one on the outside and a lower one at inner radius (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM reconstruction shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The AFV1 membrane is most likely a two-dimensional fluid.
source: It is unlikely that any details of the membrane structure are lost due to the fact that either the helical symmetry of the nucleocapsid has been imposed upon the membrane (Figure 3a) or the membrane has been cylindrically averaged (Figure 7a) since the membrane is most likely a two-dimensional fluid.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of lipid membranes and the lack of ordered features in the data.

claim: In SIRV2, the radius of the DNA is ~60 Å, while in AFV1 the supercoiling is tighter and the radius is ~30 Å.
source: In SIRV2, the radius of the DNA is ~60 Å, while in AFV1 the supercoiling is tighter and the radius is ~30 Å.
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM reconstructions of both viruses.

claim: The twist of the A-form DNA in SIRV2 is 11.2 bp/turn.
source: The twist of the A-form DNA in SIRV2 is 11.2 bp/turn (DiMaio et al., 2015) while in AFV1 it is 10.8 bp/turn: in 10 right-handed turns of the 43 Å pitch AFV1 helix, there are 93 repeats of the DNA, each with 12 bp, so there are 1116 bp per 103 (=93 + 10) right handed turns.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work on SIRV2.

claim: The twist of the A-form DNA in AFV1 is 10.8 bp/turn.
source: The twist of the A-form DNA in SIRV2 is 11.2 bp/turn (DiMaio et al., 2015) while in AFV1 it is 10.8 bp/turn: in 10 right-handed turns of the 43 Å pitch AFV1 helix, there are 93 repeats of the DNA, each with 12 bp, so there are 1116 bp per 103 (=93 + 10) right handed turns.
evidence: This is calculated from the cryo-EM reconstruction of AFV1.

claim: The helical pitch in both SIRV2 and AFV1 is ~42–43 Å.
source: Interestingly, the helical pitch in both SIRV2 and AFV1 is ~42–43 Å, but in SIRV2 there are 14.7 homodimers per turn, while in AFV1 there are only 9.3 heterodimers.
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM reconstructions of both viruses.

claim: In SIRV2 there are 14.7 homodimers per turn, while in AFV1 there are only 9.3 heterodimers.
source: Interestingly, the helical pitch in both SIRV2 and AFV1 is ~42–43 Å, but in SIRV2 there are 14.7 homodimers per turn, while in AFV1 there are only 9.3 heterodimers.
evidence: This is calculated from the cryo-EM reconstructions of both viruses.

claim: The looser packing in AFV1 appears responsible for the greater flexibility and disorder.
source: It is this looser packing in AFV1 that appears responsible for the greater flexibility and disorder.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison between AFV1 and SIRV2.

claim: SIRV2 has a linear dsDNA genome of 35,450 kb.
source: It also explains why the two viruses with linear dsDNA genomes of very different sizes – 35,450 kb for SIRV2 (Peng et al., 2001) and 20,080 for AFV1 (Bettstetter et al., 2003) – have virions of approximately the same length (about 900 nm).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: AFV1 has a linear dsDNA genome of 20,080 bp.
source: It also explains why the two viruses with linear dsDNA genomes of very different sizes – 35,450 kb for SIRV2 (Peng et al., 2001) and 20,080 for AFV1 (Bettstetter et al., 2003) – have virions of approximately the same length (about 900 nm).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: SIRV2 and AFV1 virions have approximately the same length (about 900 nm).
source: It also explains why the two viruses with linear dsDNA genomes of very different sizes – 35,450 kb for SIRV2 (Peng et al., 2001) and 20,080 for AFV1 (Bettstetter et al., 2003) – have virions of approximately the same length (about 900 nm).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the structural data.

claim: In SIRV2 there are tight contacts across the helical turns, while in AFV1 such contacts are absent.
source: In SIRV2 there are tight contacts across the helical turns, while in AFV1 such contacts are absent (Figure 3b), allowing the virions to bend, extend, and compress.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The absence of tight contacts across helical turns in AFV1 allows the virions to bend, extend, and compress.
source: In SIRV2 there are tight contacts across the helical turns, while in AFV1 such contacts are absent (Figure 3b), allowing the virions to bend, extend, and compress.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison.

claim: Due to looser protein packing, the AFV1 genome is not completely covered by the protein, while it is in SIRV2.
source: At the same time, due to looser protein packing, the AFV1 genome is not completely covered by the protein, while it is in SIRV2.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structures of both viruses.

claim: The lipid envelope provides necessary protection to the AFV1 genome in the highly acidic environment of the natural habitat.
source: Consequently, the lipid envelope provides a necessary protection to the AFV1 genome in the highly acidic environment of the natural habitat, rationalizing the presence of the envelope in lipothrixviruses.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural findings and the environmental conditions.

claim: When the membrane is removed, AFV1 virions become much more flexible.
source: When the membrane is removed (we assume as an artifact of specimen preparation) the virions become much more flexible (Figure 1).
evidence: This is observed in cryo-EM images shown in Figure 1.

claim: The presence of the membrane constrains the protein and thus indirectly imparts rigidity to the AFV1 structure.
source: Since the membrane, which has fluid-like properties, is unlikely to be directly responsible for the increased rigidity of the enveloped virions, it suggests that the presence of the membrane constrains the protein and thus indirectly imparts rigidity to the structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that membrane removal increases flexibility.

claim: The two AFV1 capsid proteins form a pseudo-symmetric heterodimer that resembles in many ways the symmetric homodimer found in SIRV2.
source: Surprisingly, we find that the two capsid proteins form a pseudo-symmetric heterodimer (Figure 3d) that resembles in many ways the symmetric homodimer found in SIRV2 (Figure 3e), and that both interact with the DNA in an equivalent manner.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3d and 3e.

claim: Both AFV1 capsid proteins interact with the DNA in an equivalent manner.
source: Surprisingly, we find that the two capsid proteins form a pseudo-symmetric heterodimer (Figure 3d) that resembles in many ways the symmetric homodimer found in SIRV2 (Figure 3e), and that both interact with the DNA in an equivalent manner.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: All amino acids in the two AFV1 capsid proteins have been accounted for with the exception of 5 N-terminal residues in both MCP1 and MCP2.
source: We have accounted for all of the amino acids in the two capsid proteins with the exception of 5 N-terminal residues in both MCP1 and MCP2.
evidence: This is stated based on the atomic model building.

claim: The 5 N-terminal residues in both MCP1 and MCP2 would be too far from the membrane to contact it.
source: However, these residues would be too far from the membrane to contact it.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model.

claim: No density extending from the protein to the membrane is observed in AFV1.
source: Further, we see no density extending from the protein to the membrane.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: In SIRV2, the N-terminal tail forms a long helix with a kink that allows it to continuously wrap around the DNA.
source: There are two main differences between the AFV1 and SIRV2 dimers: (1) In SIRV2 the N-terminal tail forms a long helix with a kink that allows it to continuously wrap around the DNA (Figure 3e), while in AFV1 the N-terminal region of both MCP1 and MCP2 form helix-turn-helix motifs which fold back to cover the DNA on both sides (Figure 3d);
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3e.

claim: In AFV1, the N-terminal region of both MCP1 and MCP2 form helix-turn-helix motifs which fold back to cover the DNA on both sides.
source: There are two main differences between the AFV1 and SIRV2 dimers: (1) In SIRV2 the N-terminal tail forms a long helix with a kink that allows it to continuously wrap around the DNA (Figure 3e), while in AFV1 the N-terminal region of both MCP1 and MCP2 form helix-turn-helix motifs which fold back to cover the DNA on both sides (Figure 3d);
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In SIRV2, the 2-fold axis of the dimer is perpendicular to the helical axis and goes through the 2-fold axis in the DNA, generating an overall bipolar symmetry for the virion.
source: (2) In SIRV2 the 2-fold axis of the dimer is perpendicular to the helical axis (and goes through the 2-fold axis in the DNA), generating an overall bipolar symmetry for the virion, while in AFV1 the pseudo-2-fold axis of the heterodimer is tilted by 25.7° and does not intersect the helical axis, so that the virion has an overall polarity visible at fairly low resolution.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure of SIRV2.

claim: In AFV1, the pseudo-2-fold axis of the heterodimer is tilted by 25.7° and does not intersect the helical axis.
source: (2) In SIRV2 the 2-fold axis of the dimer is perpendicular to the helical axis (and goes through the 2-fold axis in the DNA), generating an overall bipolar symmetry for the virion, while in AFV1 the pseudo-2-fold axis of the heterodimer is tilted by 25.7° and does not intersect the helical axis, so that the virion has an overall polarity visible at fairly low resolution.
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM structure of AFV1.

claim: The AFV1 virion has an overall polarity visible at fairly low resolution.
source: (2) In SIRV2 the 2-fold axis of the dimer is perpendicular to the helical axis (and goes through the 2-fold axis in the DNA), generating an overall bipolar symmetry for the virion, while in AFV1 the pseudo-2-fold axis of the heterodimer is tilted by 25.7° and does not intersect the helical axis, so that the virion has an overall polarity visible at fairly low resolution.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: A positive Coulombic potential surrounds the negatively-charged phosphate backbones of the DNA in AFV1.
source: Details of the wrapping of the A-form DNA by the heterodimer are shown in Figure 5, where it can be seen that a positive Coulombic potential would surround the negatively-charged phosphate backbones of the DNA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 based on the atomic model.

claim: There is a striking difference in the distribution of lipids found in the host compared to those found in the AFV1 virion membrane.
source: Since the membrane lipids would not be synthesized by the virus but must come from the host, we first compared the distribution of lipids (Figure 6a) found in the host with those found in the virion membrane (Figure 6b). There is a striking difference in the distributions showing that the incorporation of the glycerol dibiphytanyl glycerol tetraether (GDGT) lipids from the host is highly selective.
evidence: This is shown by lipid analysis data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The incorporation of GDGT lipids from the host into the AFV1 membrane is highly selective.
source: There is a striking difference in the distributions showing that the incorporation of the glycerol dibiphytanyl glycerol tetraether (GDGT) lipids from the host is highly selective.
evidence: This is concluded from the lipid composition analysis.

claim: The single most dominant lipid species in the host is GDGT-4 (containing 4 cyclopentane moieties).
source: While the single most dominant species in the host is GDGT-4 (containing 4 cyclopentane moieties), in the virion it is GDGT-0 (containing no cyclopentane moieties), found as only a few percent of the total host membrane lipids.
evidence: This is shown by lipid analysis data.

claim: The single most dominant lipid species in the AFV1 virion is GDGT-0 (containing no cyclopentane moieties).
source: While the single most dominant species in the host is GDGT-4 (containing 4 cyclopentane moieties), in the virion it is GDGT-0 (containing no cyclopentane moieties), found as only a few percent of the total host membrane lipids.
evidence: This is shown by lipid analysis data.

claim: GDGT-0 is found as only a few percent of the total host membrane lipids.
source: While the single most dominant species in the host is GDGT-4 (containing 4 cyclopentane moieties), in the virion it is GDGT-0 (containing no cyclopentane moieties), found as only a few percent of the total host membrane lipids.
evidence: This is shown by lipid analysis data.

claim: GDGT-0 is one of the most common archaeal membrane lipids.
source: Nevertheless, GDGT-0 is actually one of the most common archaeal membrane lipids (Schouten et al., 2013; Villanueva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: GDGT-0 is generally the dominant, or one of the dominant, archaeal lipids in environmental samples taken from soils, rivers, lakes and oceans accounting for >40% of all GDGTs detected.
source: Furthermore, it is generally the dominant, or one of the dominant, archaeal lipids in environmental samples taken from soils, rivers, lakes and oceans accounting for >40% of all GDGTs detected (Schouten et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Selective incorporation of host lipids in a viral membrane has previously been described in influenza budding from mammalian cells.
source: The selective incorporation of host lipids in a viral membrane has previously been described, for example, in influenza budding from mammalian cells (Gerl et al., 2012), or in a virus budding from algae (Maat et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Selective incorporation of host lipids in a viral membrane has previously been described in a virus budding from algae.
source: The selective incorporation of host lipids in a viral membrane has previously been described, for example, in influenza budding from mammalian cells (Gerl et al., 2012), or in a virus budding from algae (Maat et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: GDGT-0 is more flexible than the cyclopentane-containing GDGT lipids.
source: Because GDGT-0 is more flexible than the cyclopentane-containing GDGT lipids (Schwarzmann et al., 2015), it can better adopt the horseshoe conformations that have a lower free energy in the highly curved AFV-1 envelope (Galimzyanov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: GDGT-0 can better adopt horseshoe conformations that have a lower free energy in the highly curved AFV-1 envelope.
source: Because GDGT-0 is more flexible than the cyclopentane-containing GDGT lipids (Schwarzmann et al., 2015), it can better adopt the horseshoe conformations that have a lower free energy in the highly curved AFV-1 envelope (Galimzyanov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Selective partitioning of GDGT lipids due to the curvature of the envelope is the mechanism for GDGT-0 enrichment in the AFV-1 membrane.
source: We therefore hypothesize that selective partitioning of GDGT lipids due to the curvature of the envelope is the mechanism for GDGT-0 enrichment in the AFV-1 membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the structural and lipid composition data.

claim: Multiple simulations were performed of GDGT-0 lipids arranged cylindrically around the capsid assembly in different densities and orientations.
source: Knowing the lipid composition of the virion, we used molecular dynamics (MD) to model the viral membrane. Multiple simulations were performed of GDGT-0 lipids arranged cylindrically around the capsid assembly in different densities and orientations.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used.

claim: GDGT-0 lipids frequently adopted a U-shaped or horseshoe conformation in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Lipids were modeled with a single phosphoinositol headgroup, as this is the smallest headgroup commonly found on GDGT lipids in the A. hospitalis host (the others are dihexose and sulfonated trihexose headgroups). These lipids frequently adopted a U-shaped or horseshoe conformation, and these horseshoe-rich envelopes with a mix of 'inward-facing' and 'outward-facing' lipids were the only ones that stably maintained the curvature and thickness observed in the radial density profile from cryo-EM.
evidence: This is observed from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Horseshoe-rich envelopes with a mix of 'inward-facing' and 'outward-facing' lipids were the only ones that stably maintained the curvature and thickness observed in the radial density profile from cryo-EM.
source: These lipids frequently adopted a U-shaped or horseshoe conformation, and these horseshoe-rich envelopes with a mix of 'inward-facing' and 'outward-facing' lipids were the only ones that stably maintained the curvature and thickness observed in the radial density profile from cryo-EM.
evidence: This is concluded from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The best-fit arrangement of lipids in the AFV1 envelope features 40% of lipids with headgroups facing inwards towards the nucleocapsid and 60% of lipids with headgroups facing towards the outside.
source: A horseshoe lipid conformation from simulation was therefore used to fit the cryo-EM radial density profile; the best-fit arrangement features 40% of lipids with headgroups facing inwards towards the nucleocapsid and 60% of lipids with headgroups facing towards the outside (Figure 7).
evidence: This is determined by fitting simulation data to cryo-EM density profile shown in Figure 7.

claim: Structural models simulated with 40% inward-facing and 60% outward-facing lipid orientation maintained a stable envelope structure with the thickness, curvature, propensity to horseshoe conformations, and the slight ~8 Å water-filled gap between envelope and capsid observed by cryo-EM.
source: Structural models simulated with this lipid orientation maintained a stable envelope structure with the thickness, curvature, propensity to horseshoe conformations, and the slight ~8 Å water-filled gap between envelope and capsid observed by cryo-EM, similar to a surface-supported membrane.
evidence: This is observed from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The density in the gap between envelope and capsid observed by cryo-EM was the same as the solvent outside the virus.
source: The density in this gap observed by cryo-EM was the same as the solvent outside the virus, further suggesting that the region between the envelope and the polar capsid surface and the envelope is similar to that between a supported lipid bilayer and its planar support (Ajo-Franklin et al., 2005; Koenig et al., 1996).
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM density.

claim: The region between the envelope and the polar capsid surface is similar to that between a supported lipid bilayer and its planar support.
source: The density in this gap observed by cryo-EM was the same as the solvent outside the virus, further suggesting that the region between the envelope and the polar capsid surface and the envelope is similar to that between a supported lipid bilayer and its planar support (Ajo-Franklin et al., 2005; Koenig et al., 1996).
evidence: This is inferred from the density observations and cited previous work.

claim: The lipid composition of Acidianus hospitalis is very similar to that previously determined in Sulfolobus solfataricus.
source: The lipid composition of Acidianus hospitalis, which we report in this study, is very similar to that previously determined in a related organism, Sulfolobus solfataricus (Quemin et al., 2015) which has a ~5 nm-thick membrane.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Sulfolobus solfataricus has a ~5 nm-thick membrane.
source: The lipid composition of Acidianus hospitalis, which we report in this study, is very similar to that previously determined in a related organism, Sulfolobus solfataricus (Quemin et al., 2015) which has a ~5 nm-thick membrane.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: A spindle-shaped virus SSV1 released from Sulfolobus cells by budding has a membrane enriched in GDGT-0 which is considerably thinner compared to the host membrane.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown that a spindle-shaped virus SSV1 released from Sulfolobus cells by budding, similar to AFV1, has a membrane enriched in GDGT-0 which is also considerably thinner compared to the host membrane (Quemin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: The lipid conformation described in AFV1 might be more general in enveloped viruses of archaea.
source: It thus appears that the lipid conformation described in our current study might be more general in enveloped viruses of archaea.
evidence: This is speculated based on the SSV1 findings.

claim: A number of in vitro studies have described archaeal lipids forming U-shaped structures at an air-water interface.
source: A number of in vitro studies have described archaeal lipids forming U-shaped structures at an air-water interface (Gliozzi et al., 1994; Köhler et al., 2006; Melikyan et al., 1991; Patwardhan and Thompson, 2000; Tomoaia-Cotisel et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The presence of cyclopentane rings has been suggested to rigidify the lipids, making them unable to form a horseshoe.
source: The presence of cyclopentane rings (found in the main host species, GDGT-4) has been suggested to rigidify the lipids, making them unable to form a horseshoe (Gliozzi et al., 1994), in agreement with another study which found that more rigid tetraether lipids could not form a horseshoe at the air-water interface while the more flexible lipids did (Patwardhan and Thompson, 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Theoretical studies suggest that membranes formed from horseshoe conformation lipids have lower curvature energies.
source: Furthermore, theoretical studies suggest that membranes formed from horseshoe conformation lipids have lower curvature energies (Galimzyanov et al., 2016) and would thus be energetically favored on the highly curved AFV-1 surface.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Lower curvature energies of horseshoe conformation lipids may be the main driving force for the exquisite selectivity seen for the incorporation of host lipids in the viral membrane.
source: This may be the main driving force for the exquisite selectivity seen for the incorporation of host lipids in the viral membrane.
evidence: This is speculated based on theoretical considerations.

claim: A biological role for the horseshoe lipid conformation has not previously been suggested or found.
source: A biological role for such a horseshoe conformation has not previously been suggested or found.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in previous knowledge.

claim: Besides the canonical bacterial/eukaryotic membrane bilayer and archaeal monolayer, there is a third type of biological membrane, the viral horseshoe membrane layer.
source: Our study demonstrates that besides the canonical bacterial/eukaryotic membrane bilayer and archaeal monolayer, there is a third type of biological membrane, the viral horse-shoe membrane layer.
evidence: This is concluded from the findings of the study.

claim: Archaeal lipids have been shown to resist phospholipases, extremes of temperature and pH, and can even survive autoclaving.
source: Since the archaeal lipids have been shown to resist phospholipases, extremes of temperature and pH, and can even survive autoclaving, the membrane described here has many potential applications (Patel and Sprott, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: The molecular dynamics simulations predicted that the membrane would account for ~43% of the total mass of the virion.
source: The models also predicted that the membrane would account for ~43% of the total mass of the virion, in excellent agreement with the ~40% estimate from the cryo-EM density integration.
evidence: This is calculated from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The cryo-EM map was deposited in the EMDB with accession number EMD-8780.
source: The cryo-EM map was deposited in the EMDB with accession number EMD-8780, and the atomic model was deposited in the PDB with accession number 5W7G.
evidence: This is stated as a data deposition record.

claim: The atomic model was deposited in the PDB with accession number 5W7G.
source: The cryo-EM map was deposited in the EMDB with accession number EMD-8780, and the atomic model was deposited in the PDB with accession number 5W7G.
evidence: This is stated as a data deposition record.
